turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry, before you start, the partner is on the phone out at reception. They said the shaking went on about twenty minutes, and that you went very pale on the train.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit down. You're very welcome. What brought you along?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. I was on the train yesterday evening and my chest went all tight, and I thought I was having a heart attack.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): God, that sounds desperate. Tell me how it felt, in your own words.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): It just came over me. Tight across the chest, I was shaking, and there was this awful fear. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Had you ever had a turn like that before?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Never. I'm usually grand.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long did it last, would you say?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Err. I don't know, doctor. Maybe ten minutes. The carriage was packed and roasting, sure, but that's nothing to do with it.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. The partner has it at twenty minutes. We'll say somewhere between ten and twenty minutes so.
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm. Yeah. Could be.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the chest still tight now, or has it passed?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): It's gone. Chest is grand. I'm just wrecked, I didn't sleep a wink after it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you black out, or feel you might fall?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I stayed standing. Held onto the pole.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did it go down the arm, or up into the jaw?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nowhere else. Just the chest.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you short of breath with it?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. I couldn't get a proper breath. Like a band around me.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you clammy, or sick in the stomach?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Clammy, yeah. Not sick. I wasn't going to get sick.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): And was the heart racing?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. It was thumping, going very fast.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on at the minute?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. My sugar tablets, the Metformine, 500 twice a day. And Omprazole 20 milligrams in the morning, for the burn in the stomach.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything for the blood pressure, or an inhaler?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh, Mizartan for the pressure. Maybe 40 milligrams. I don't know, doctor, the dose could be wrong. And the purple inhaler when I get wheezy, not every day.
[SEG0028] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): The partner wanted that passed on as well. They said the Mizartan is for the pressure, but they didn't know the strength.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's it. I pick them up at the chemist.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or take cocaine or any other drugs?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I don't smoke, and I don't take drugs. Never have.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. I'll have a listen to your heart and your lungs.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal. The lungs are clear, no wheeze today.
[SEG0034] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Vitals from the cubicle. Pulse 88, blood pressure 122 over 78, and the oxygen is 98 percent.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Those numbers are sound. I think this was a panic attack, the first one, not a heart attack. I can't completely rule out a heart rhythm problem until we see a tracing.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): So I'm not dying then? I don't know, doctor. It really felt like it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're not dying. We'll do an ECG this morning and they'll call you down for it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): And a breath for if it starts again. In for four, hold for four, out for six. Practise that twice a day when you're calm, and use it if the fear comes on the train.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Four, four and six. Of. I'll try. I missed my stop yesterday with the fuss, which was gas afterwards.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks and we'll look at the ECG together. If the tightness comes back and you can't settle it, go straight to A&E, don't be waiting on it.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Grand. Thanks a million.

spec.situation: Young adult after a first episode of sudden chest tightness, shaking and fear on a train; thinks it was a heart attack; no drugs; partner phones in details; doctor orders ECG, teaches breathing.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
